claims.claim: Nicolas Appert developed a method of cooking food, sealing it in glass jars, and reheating the sealed containers, and was awarded the French government prize in 1810.
claims.episode_span: Nicolas Appert responded by cooking food, sealing it in glass jars, and heating the sealed containers again, a method that won a French government prize in 1810.
claims.supporting_quote: In 1809, Nicolas Appert , a French confectioner and brewer, observed that food cooked inside a jar did not spoil unless the seals leaked, and developed a method of sealing food in glass jars. [ 5 ] Appert was awarded the prize in 1810 by Count Montelivert, a French minister of the interior.

claims.claim: The French government had offered a 12,000-franc award for a cheap, effective method of preserving large amounts of food for its army.
claims.episode_span: a method that won a French government prize in 1810
claims.supporting_quote: the French government offered a hefty cash award of 12,000 francs to any inventor who could devise a cheap and effective method of preserving large amounts of food to create well-preserved military rations for the Grande Armée

claims.claim: Appert did not know why his method worked; Louis Pasteur demonstrated the role of microbes in food spoilage about 50 years later.
claims.episode_span: He did not know about microbes; he simply tested whether excluding air and applying heat would stop whatever caused rot.
claims.supporting_quote: The reason for lack of spoilage was unknown at the time, since it would be another 50 years before Louis Pasteur demonstrated the role of microbes in food spoilage and developed pasteurization

claims.claim: Canned meat was being sold to the British Army and Royal Navy by 1817, consistent with canned goods reaching the British Navy by the 1820s.
claims.episode_span: canned goods reached the British Navy by the 1820s and civilian markets shortly afterward
claims.supporting_quote: The main market for the food at this stage was the British Army and Royal Navy . By 1817, Donkin recorded that he had sold £3000 (equal to £ 222,201 today) worth of canned meat in six months.

claims.claim: Early canning was slow and labour-intensive: each large can was hand-made and took up to six hours to cook, keeping canned food expensive.
claims.episode_span: early cans were soldered by hand, which limited throughput until later mechanization addressed that bottleneck
claims.supporting_quote: Initially, the canning process was slow and labour-intensive, as each large can had to be hand-made, and took up to six hours to cook, making canned food too expensive for ordinary people.

claims.claim: Early can manufacture used poisonous lead solder for sealing, a genuine contamination path.
claims.episode_span: early cans were heavy, the solder sometimes contaminated contents, and the process could not yet handle every food without texture or flavor change
claims.supporting_quote: Early methods of manufacture employed poisonous lead solder for sealing the cans.
